passages.text: And do not say, “He acted impiously toward the wise by hiding these things from them.” Far be it from us to suppose this. For he did not act impiously. Rather, because they hid the knowledge of the kingdom and neither entered themselves nor allowed those who wished to enter, for this reason, in accordance with justice, just as they themselves hid the ways from those who wished, so the secrets were also hidden from them. This was so that what they had done might happen likewise to them, and with the measure they measured, it might be measured to them equally. For the worthy person is owed knowledge of what he does not know; but from the unworthy person it is taken away, even if he seems to possess it and is wise in other matters, and given to the worthy, even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τῆς μαθητείας ὦσιν νήπιοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Infants here is explicitly qualified by time in discipleship, not necessarily literal nursing children. The metaphor is retained rather than silently harmonizing all infant-language.

passages.text: If someone says, “Nothing was hidden from the sons of Israel, because it is written, ‘Nothing escaped you, Israel; for do not say, Jacob, “The way was hidden from me,”’” one must understand that the matters important to the kingdom were hidden from them, but the way leading into the kingdom, which is a manner of life, was not hidden. This is why he also says, “For do not say that the way was hidden from me.” The way is the manner of life, since Moses too says, “Look, I have set before your face the way of life and the way of death.” In agreement the teacher said, “Enter through the narrow and constricted way, through which you will enter life.” Elsewhere, when someone asked, “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” he pointed out the law’s commandments.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which is a manner of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here is conduct or way of living, not a political constitution.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τῆς στενῆς καὶ τεθλιμμένης ὁδοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: through the narrow and constricted way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains way as quoted here, not an imported gate from another witness.

passages.text: From Isaiah’s saying in God’s person, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” it does not follow that Isaiah too was hinting at a God other than the known maker. Rather, through a different riddle he called the known one unknown, because the people, ignorant of the known God’s just disposition, sinned and did not suppose that they would be judged by the good God. Therefore, after saying, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” he added, “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins.” For, as I said, through ignorance of his justice they were without fear and became full of sins, supposing him only good, in the sense that he would not pursue their sins.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the disposition/character sense; the argument concerns ignorance of justice, not ignorance that any deity exists.
Keeps the restrictive only, which is central to the polemic against separating goodness from judgment.

passages.text: Some sinned in this way from the supposition that, because of his goodness, he does not judge; others from the opposite view. For, supposing the statements of the scriptures against God to be true, although they are unjust and false, they did not know his true divinity and power. Therefore, supposing that he is ignorant, delights in murders, lets the wicked off through gifts of sacrifices, and also deceives, lies, and does everything unjust, they themselves, doing things like God, insisted while sinning that they were acting reverently. Therefore they were immovable toward what is better, and when admonished did not turn back. For they had no fear, considering themselves made like God through such actions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς γὰρ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν γραφῶν φωνάς, ἀδίκους οὔσας καὶ ψευδεῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the statements of the scriptures against God ... although they are unjust and false
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the historical speaker’s explicit criticism of certain scriptural statements. It is neither softened nor presented as the translator’s own verdict about scripture.
Retains the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

passages.text: One might reasonably say that the words, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father,” were addressed to those who supposed him to be like this. And rightly so. For had they known, they would not have sinned by believing books really written against God for testing. Elsewhere too, wishing to show them more clearly the cause of their error, he says, “This is why you are deceived: you do not know the true things in the scriptures, and for this reason you are also ignorant of God’s power.” Therefore every person who wants to be saved must become, as the teacher said, a judge of the books written for testing. For he said this: “Become approved money changers.” Money changers are needed because the counterfeit is also mixed in with the genuine.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the true things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinction within the scriptures asserted by the author; it is not replaced by simply the scriptures.
πειρασμός can mean testing or temptation. The argument treats problematic books as a test of discernment; the temptation alternative remains possible.
Retains the money-changing analogy and the approved/genuine versus counterfeit contrast.
